subject: control.mode with restart = TRUE produces worse fit than with initial mode

messages.author: 216dc199b6cf5729
messages.subject: control.mode with restart = TRUE produces worse fit than with initial mode
parts:
Hello

When fitting a model with prescribed initial conditions of the mode I get a worse fit, i.e. much higher DIC and higher WAIC, when setting restart = TRUE compared to just using the initial mode (theta.ini obtained from a fitting a subset of the data).
It behaves like optimizing away from near optimum.

How can I help INLA to discover the proper mode?
I experimented with control.inla strategy settings, but those do not make any difference to the value and the log-likelihood of the reported mode.
What can I look at, to see where this issue comes from?

Details:
The model is the same between two fits:
inla(formula = formula, data = inla.stack.data(st.est), control.compute = list(config = TRUE, 
 dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE), control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE, 
 A = inla.stack.A(st.est), 
   link = 1), control.family = list(control.link = list(model = "log"), 
 hyper = list(prec = priorOrigPrec)), control.inla = control.inla, 
 control.results = control.results, control.mode  = ..1)

y ~ 0 + f(mu, model = "rw1", constr = FALSE, hyper = list(prec = list(fixed = TRUE, 
    initial = 3.2188758248682)), values = predMu) + f(i, model = spde, 
    group = i.group, control.group = list(model = "iid")) + f(idx, 
    hyper = list(prec = priorLogPrec))

Fitting a smooth function of time (rw1) + smooth time (SPDE-1D) group effect function with iid group model + 
a random error for eta and a log link function for soil CO2 efflux time series of four replicates.


The only difference between the two fits is the entry restart of the argument to control.mode:
str(ctrl.modeFit2) # prescribe mode 
List of 3
 $ theta  : num [1:4] 1.71 5.52 -1.95 3.86
 $ x      : num [1:110511] 1.098 0.929 0.588 1.001 0.753 ...
 $ restart: logi FALSE


str(ctrl.modeFit)  # search mode starting from prescribed initial values
List of 3    
 $ theta  : num [1:4] 1.71 5.52 -1.95 3.86
 $ x      : num [1:110511] 1.098 0.929 0.588 1.001 0.753 ...
 $ restart: logi TRUE

And the corresponding DIC: 
[1]  27234.11 167126.81

And the modes of the fitted objects:
List of 5
 $ theta             : Named num [1:4] 1.71 5.52 -1.95 3.86
  ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
 $ x                 : num [1:110511] 1.098 0.929 0.588 1.001 0.753 ...
 $ theta.tags        : chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
 $ mode.status       : num 4
 $ log.posterior.mode: num -46674

List of 5
 $ theta             : Named num [1:4] 1.73 5.36 -1.92 4.01
  ..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
 $ x                 : num [1:110511] 0.3606 0.1909 0.0962 0.3203 0.1368 ...
 $ theta.tags        : chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
 $ mode.status       : num 3
 $ log.posterior.mode: num -159875

The log-likelihood with the restart option gets much worse.
The hyperparameters are quite similar, but the x are quite different.
Where can I find documentation on 'mode.status'?

I am running on an Ubuntu Server using RStudio-web and INLA version 19.10.16

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] control.mode with restart = TRUE produces worse fit than with initial mode
parts:
Hi,

that was no good. I kind of guess that you have a pretty flat
posterior and then the optimizer have some issues finding the mode.

If this is a 'feature' of the model, then I usually do

r = inla(...)
r = inla.rerun(r)

to make sure its stable. You can also increase the accuracy in the
inner optimization, like

control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-10)

If you do not expect a flat posterior, then tighting the model in
terms of more informative priors will do wonders.

Otherwise, send me stuff so I can rerun it here...

H

messages.subject: RE: Re: [r-inla] control.mode with restart = TRUE produces worse fit than with initial mode
parts:
I have noticed this as well with binomial models, not so much in that it produces worse results (sometimes they are better) but that supplying different initial values frequently results in a different posterior than sticking with the defaults.  Both are often good, but they are nonetheless different.  On the one hand, no matter where you start, the results seem to be repeatable from that starting point, so that is good.  On the other hand, it would nice if initial values only affected optimization time (which is what I had assumed) rather than the result.  It’s almost  as if finding the mode in high dimensions can be tricky!

 

Perhaps the solution is tightening the tolerance criteria as H suggests.  Of course, we don’t want that to slow things down too much either.  Perhaps there is a happy medium.  I will give that a try.

 

On a separate but perhaps related note, the initial value seems to make all the difference with the experimental robit link (thank you again for adding that) but I suspect that is because that link is tricky to estimate and part of the specification may just involve working backward from a good initial estimate.  

 

Jonathan

messages.author: 216dc199b6cf5729
messages.subject: Re: control.mode with restart = TRUE produces worse fit than with initial mode
parts:
Dear Håvard Rue and Jonathan,

thanks for looking into this.

I was not expecting a very flat prior because the model was constrained for
several other data-sets. However, the "r2 <- inla.rerun(r)" took nearly more than 40 minutes
longer than the original fit. And indeed, both theta and x changed quite
a bit. So its unstable for this specific data-set.

I reran the model with "control.inla$tolerance <- 1e-10".
And got the same result as with the original run:
str(r$mode)

List of 5
$ theta : Named num [1:4] 1.73 5.36 -1.92 4.01
..- attr(*, "names")= chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
$ x : num [1:110511] 0.3606 0.1909 0.0962 0.3203 0.1368 ...
$ theta.tags : chr [1:4] "Log precision for the Gaussian observations" "log(Range) for i" "log(Stdev) for i" "Log precision for idx"
$ mode.status : num 3
$ log.posterior.mode: num -159875

Hence, constraining the tolerance did not help so far.

I uploaded my setup to
https://we.tl/t-Bk082wFdGA
It contains the function within the more complex setup (of a automated measurement processing workflow) which calls the INLA
model and a dump.frames() object so that the state inside this function can be recovered. The control.mode argument is given with the "...": str(list(...))

Before fitting I need to say for the long time series:
m = get("inla.models", INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv());m$latent$rw1$min.diff
<- 1e-6; assign("inla.models", m, INLA:::inla.get.inlaEnv())

Yours
Thomas

parts:
On Wed, 2020-02-12 at 08:54 -0600, bach...@gmail.com wrote:
>
> Perhaps the solution is tightening the tolerance criteria as H
> suggests. Of course, we don’t want that to slow things down too
> much either. Perhaps there is a happy medium. I will give that a
> try.

yes, reducing tolerance and using the

r = inla.rerun(r)

feature, are my best guesses.

In some cases, tuning initial values will help. In general, it seems
to be benefitial to start with a very tight model and losen it up,
instead of the other way around.

I must admit, that optimisation problems are often a sign of something
else (!!!!), like a very weakly identified model because of weak data
or a simply to complex model with 'weak' priors...

H

--
Håvard Rue

There is another parameter as well


control.inla=list(h=...)

which is the step-size for the hyperparameters, you may try to reduce
that one a little from the default 0.01, to 0.001, f.ex. If its to
low, then numerical issues will kick in as well...

H
